entities.date_note: The HK6 elite cemetery runs from about Naqada IIA through Naqada IIIC1. Dating is by Naqada-phase placement rather than radiocarbon, so sub-century precision for individual tombs should not be trusted.

caveats.text: Predynastic Egypt is often told as one centre rising. Hierakonpolis, Abydos and Naqada were competing or complementary centres, not a single seat of authority.

entities.summary: An Upper Egyptian power centre with monumental elite tombs, industrial-scale brewing, and buried elephants.

entities.name: Tomb U-j at Abydos
entities.date_note: Radiocarbon on wood from the tomb: Hd-12953 at 4470+/-30 BP calibrating to 3310-3230, 3180-3160 and 3120-3030 cal BC; Hd-12954 at 4595+/-25 BP giving 3490-3470 and 3380-3330 cal BC. Related Naqada IIIa2 tombs cluster around 3510-3100 cal BC.

caveats.text: Whether Egyptian writing was invented independently or prompted by contact with Mesopotamia is not settled. The dates are close enough that neither priority nor influence can be demonstrated.

entities.summary: The richest tomb at Abydos before the First Dynasty, holding the earliest known Egyptian writing.

entities.name: Dynasty 0
entities.date_note: A modern historiographic label, not an Egyptian one, correlated with Naqada IIIB. The succession Iry-Hor, then Ka, then Narmer may include overlapping reigns.

caveats.text: Dynasty 0 and Dynasty 00 are not standardised. Scholars draw the boundaries differently, and the order of the earliest rulers, known mainly from serekhs on pots, is not secure.

entities.summary: The rulers before the First Dynasty — Iry-Hor, Ka, Narmer — and the best argument that unification was a process rather than a moment.

entities.name: The Narmer Palette
entities.date_note: Placed at Naqada IIIC1, about 3100 BC, on typological grounds.

alternatives.label: Records an actual conquest of the Delta
alternatives.note: The historical-event reading, associated with Yurco. Long treated as conclusive evidence for military unification under Narmer.

caveats.text: It does not date a unification or show one happened as an event. It shows a smiting-and-dual-crown kingship ideology existed by about 3100 BC.
Tell el-Farkha shows no invasion layer in the Delta, and Lower Egyptian material culture had already been absorbed gradually, centuries earlier.

entities.summary: A carved schist palette showing a king smiting an enemy, and probably the most over-read object in Egyptology.

entities.name: Merimde Beni Salama
entities.date_note: Published ranges include 5300-4200, 4900-4000, 4880-4250 and 4750-4250 BC across different research groups and sample series. The wide range here is deliberate: no tighter figure is defensible.
entities.summary: One of the largest Neolithic settlements of the Delta, and a site whose published dates disagree by five hundred years.

entities.name: El-Omari
entities.date_note: Published radiocarbon places it at the end of the northern Early Neolithic sequence, between 4600 and 4400 cal BC, with some sources extending to 4300.
entities.summary: A Lower Egyptian Neolithic settlement near Helwan, plainer in its material culture than its Upper Egyptian contemporaries.

entities.name: Maadi-Buto Culture
entities.date_note: Radiocarbon places the culture at roughly 3900-3300/3200 BC, with Buto I about 3900-3800 and the Maadi phase about 3800-3600. The transitional layer in which Naqada material replaces it falls about 3300-3200 BC.

caveats.text: This replacement is often told as the unification, coincident with Narmer. The excavated dates put it centuries earlier and show it happening gradually.

entities.summary: The last independent culture of Lower Egypt, absorbed into the expanding Naqada world well before any king unified anything.

entities.name: The Muge Shell Middens
entities.date_note: Mesolithic central Portugal is generally dated 8,500-7,000 cal BP. Deposition at Cabeco da Amoreira specifically runs 8,000-7,350 cal BP, and the first burial at Vale de Romeiras in the Sado dates to 8,543-8,334 cal BP.

caveats.text: Not a last stand before farming. The Muge and Sado foragers overlap in time with incoming Neolithic groups and interact with them for centuries.

entities.summary: Enormous mounds of estuarine shell in the Tagus and Sado valleys, used as both settlement and cemetery by foragers who overlapped with the first farmers.

entities.name: The Obanian
entities.date_note: Bulk charcoal from five Oronsay middens gave 6,200-5,400 BP uncalibrated, calibrating to about 5,150-4,250 cal BC. Bulk charcoal samples average material of different ages, so these are coarser than single-entity dates.
entities.summary: Shell middens around Oban and on Oronsay, Scotland's main evidence that late foragers there lived substantially off the sea.

entities.name: The 8.2 Kiloyear Event
entities.date_note: Dated in the NGRIP Greenland ice core by layer counting to 8,250-8,090 cal BP, which is far more precise than any of the archaeological responses being matched to it.

alternatives.label: No causal link in the Scheldt basin
alternatives.note: A multi-proxy Belgian study found little evidence connecting the 9.3 and 8.2 ka coolings to changes in human behaviour there.

caveats.text: Not a uniform catastrophe. Western Scotland shows demographic collapse, while Atlantic Iberia shows intensified shellfish use and population growth in the same window.

entities.summary: An abrupt cooling that hit Mesolithic Europe unevenly — collapse in Scotland, apparent resilience in Belgium, and growth on the Atlantic coast.

entities.name: The British Empire
entities.date_note: Neither end is a fact. The span given is the widest defensible one: Gilbert's Newfoundland claim to the Hong Kong handover, after which Britain held no significant overseas territory for the first time since 1707. Activity before the Acts of Union in 1707 was English, not British.

alternatives.label: Start 1497 (Cabot's voyage)
alternatives.note: Dates the empire from England's first overseas claim rather than any settlement.

alternatives.label: Start 1607 (Jamestown)
alternatives.note: Dates it from the first permanent settlement, the most commonly cited criterion.

alternatives.label: End 1947 (Indian independence)
alternatives.note: The most common institutional marker for the end of the imperial core.

alternatives.label: End 1956 (Suez)
alternatives.note: Diplomatic historians treat Suez as the moment imperial power was publicly exposed as spent.

caveats.text: The start is a definitional fork, not a dispute about evidence. Nobody disagrees about what happened in 1497, 1583 or 1607, only about which one counts as a beginning.
The split into a First and Second Empire hinging on 1783 is standard in tertiary sources but contested by specialists, who argue the two overlapped and the break is artificial.

entities.summary: The largest empire in history by area, and an entity whose beginning and end are both matters of definition rather than record.

entities.name: The Acts of Union
entities.date_note: Ratified 1 May 1707.
entities.summary: England and Scotland became one state, which is the point at which an English empire can properly be called British.

entities.name: Cahokia
entities.date_note: First occupied around 700 CE, with the florescence conventionally placed between about 950 and 1350.
entities.summary: The largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico, and the reason 'Mississippian' names a civilization rather than a pottery style.

entities.name: Chaco Canyon
entities.date_note: Chaco's great houses are dated by tree rings, often to the year and sometimes to the felling season -- among the most precisely dated architecture anywhere before written records.
entities.summary: The administrative and ceremonial centre of the Ancestral Puebloan world, linked by engineered roads across the San Juan Basin.

entities.name: Tenochtitlan
entities.date_note: 1325 is the traditional founding date. The city fell on 13 August 1521. It predates the Triple Alliance by a century: the capital is older than the empire it came to head.

caveats.text: 1325 is a traditional date from Mexica accounts, not an archaeological one.

entities.summary: The island capital of the Mexica, and one of the largest cities in the world when Cortés reached it.

entities.name: Monte Albán
entities.date_note: Rose to regional prominence around 500 BCE with its Classic floruit between about 300 and 900 CE.
entities.summary: The Zapotec capital on a levelled mountaintop above the Oaxaca valley.

entities.name: Tikal
entities.summary: The largest excavated Classic Maya city, and the clearest single illustration that the Maya were never one empire.

entities.name: Machu Picchu
entities.date_note: Construction is conventionally placed around 1450, in Pachacuti's reign. The site outlasts the empire: it is tied to Vilcabamba, which held out until 1572.
entities.summary: A royal estate on the Vilcabamba ridge, built under Pachacuti and abandoned within a century of Spanish arrival.

entities.name: Qhapaq Ñan
entities.date_note: Built largely under the empire but incorporating far older routes, which is why the inscribed network is described as a cultural route rather than an Inca invention.
entities.summary: The Andean road network that made the empire governable, running some 30,000 kilometres across six modern countries.

entities.name: The Netherlands
entities.summary: The Dutch Republic and its successors, and the two chartered companies through which a small state ran a global trading empire.

entities.name: Dutch East India Company
entities.date_note: Chartered 20 March 1602; the charter lapsed on 31 December 1799. The 1798, 1799 and 1800 dates in circulation are not rival claims but three steps: the Batavian Republic assumed the company's debts in March 1798, the charter lapsed at the end of 1799, and the state took administrative control in 1800.

caveats.text: Not a company in the modern sense. Its charter granted powers of war, treaty-making, coinage and colonial government.

entities.summary: A chartered company with the power to wage war, coin money and hold territory, which for two centuries was the Dutch presence in Asia.

entities.name: Dutch West India Company
entities.date_note: Chartered 3 June 1621 and declared bankrupt by the States General in September 1674. This is the first company; a second followed immediately under a near-identical charter, and sources that give '1621-1794' have run the two together.
entities.summary: The Atlantic counterpart of the VOC: Brazil, the Caribbean, New Netherland, and a dominant share of the Dutch slave trade.

entities.name: Second Dutch West India Company
entities.date_note: Chartered 1675 and wound up on 1 January 1792, having been abolished by decision in 1791.

alternatives.label: Ends 1791 (abolition decided)
alternatives.note: The States General decided not to renew the patent in 1791; the formal end followed on 1 January 1792.

alternatives.label: Ends 1794 (French invasion)
alternatives.note: Britannica dates the dissolution to the French invasion of the Dutch Republic.

entities.summary: The successor company, narrower in remit and increasingly dependent on the slave trade.

entities.name: First French Colonial Empire
entities.date_note: Both ends are choices. 1534 is Cartier's claim rather than a settlement, and the end depends on which loss counts as terminal.

alternatives.label: 1605-1803 (Port Royal to the Louisiana sale)
alternatives.note: Dates the empire from the first actual colony and ends it with the sale of Louisiana rather than the Napoleonic collapse.

entities.summary: New France, the Caribbean sugar islands and the Indian trading posts, most of it lost or sold within two generations.

entities.name: Second French Colonial Empire
entities.date_note: 1830 is the invasion of Algiers and is essentially uncontested. The end is Algerian independence, declared on 5 July 1962 -- a date chosen to fall exactly 132 years after the landing, which makes it a commemorative convention as much as an administrative fact.

caveats.text: 5 July 1962 is a symbolic date. The Evian ceasefire was in March and France recognised independence on 3 July.

entities.summary: Rebuilt around Algeria and expanded across West and Central Africa and Indochina, and dismantled in fifteen years after 1945.

entities.name: The Georgian Era
entities.date_note: 1714 is George I's accession on the death of Queen Anne. The end is disputed: 1830 with George IV, the last of the four Georges, or 1837 with William IV, which is the boundary with the Victorian era.

name_forms.name: Regency era
name_forms.note: Strictly the regency of George IV as Prince of Wales during his father's illness, though used loosely for the wider period.

alternatives.label: Ends 1830 (death of George IV)
alternatives.note: Ends the era with the last of the four kings it is named after.

entities.summary: Hanoverian Britain: the Jacobite risings, the loss of America, the Regency, and the industrial transformation that reshaped the country.

entities.name: The Columbian Exchange
entities.date_note: The end date is a convention: the exchange has no terminus, and 1700 marks roughly where the sharpest demographic phase closes. The pre-contact population, and so the scale of the collapse, is one of the least settled quantities in the discipline.

name_forms.name: Columbian Exchange
name_forms.note: Coined by Alfred Crosby in his 1972 book of that name; the phrase is younger than most of the scholarship it now organises.

name_forms.name: Great Dying
name_forms.note: Used for the depopulation specifically, and naming it separately makes clear that 'exchange' is a very mild word for it.

alternatives.label: Pre-contact population c. 90-112 million (Dobyns)
alternatives.note: Dobyns's 1966 estimate, built on an assumption of about 95 per cent epidemic mortality.

alternatives.label: Pre-contact population c. 55 million (Denevan)
alternatives.note: Denevan's 1976 middle estimate; modern work converges near 45-60 million.

caveats.text: Estimates of the pre-contact population range from 8 million to over 100 million. The disagreement is methodological, not evidentiary, so more digging does not narrow it.
'Exchange' describes crops and livestock accurately and the human consequence not at all: depopulation estimates run from 75 to 95 per cent.

entities.summary: The transfer of crops, animals, people and above all disease between hemispheres, and the demographic collapse that followed in the Americas.

entities.name: Dvaravati
entities.date_note: Whether Dvaravati was a single kingdom or a network of related polities sharing a culture is unsettled. The span is approximate at both ends; its close is especially unclear, being a gradual absorption by Khmer and then Thai power rather than a conquest.

caveats.text: Often described as a kingdom, but the evidence may support a cultural network of separate polities instead.

entities.summary: Mon Buddhist culture of the Chao Phraya basin, of disputed political unity.

entities.name: Post-Pagan Burma
entities.date_note: A period of coexisting rivals rather than one polity: Myinsaing, Pinya, Sagaing, then Ava against Mon Hanthawaddy. Entered as a single span because the dataset previously left these 213 years blank entirely, which was worse than a container.
entities.summary: Two centuries of competing successor states after Pagan fell, principally Ava in the interior and Hanthawaddy in the delta.

entities.name: Toungoo Dynasty
entities.date_note: Scholars divide it into a First and Second Toungoo, and give competing start dates; 1510 follows the founding of the Toungoo state itself rather than a later imperial expansion.

alternatives.label: Later start, dating the dynasty from its imperial phase
alternatives.note: Britannica and Wikipedia do not lead with the same year.

entities.summary: Reunified Burma and briefly built the largest empire in mainland Southeast Asia.

entities.name: Konbaung Dynasty
entities.summary: The last Burmese dynasty, ended by British annexation after the third of three Anglo-Burmese wars.

entities.name: British Burma
entities.date_note: Annexation followed the war of 1885; the formal proclamation and administrative reorganisation ran into 1886. Independence came in January 1948.

name_forms.name: Burma
name_forms.note: The colonial-era English name. Myanmar and Burma both derive from the same root, and the choice between them remains politically loaded.

entities.summary: Annexed after the Third Anglo-Burmese War and governed as a province of British India until 1937.

entities.name: Sukhothai Kingdom
entities.date_note: Both the 1238 founding date and the 'first Thai kingdom' framing rest on the Ram Khamhaeng inscription, whose authenticity Michael Vickery and others have questioned. Treat the date as traditional rather than attested. Absorbed by Ayutthaya in 1438.

alternatives.label: 1238, from the Ram Khamhaeng inscription
alternatives.note: The inscription's authenticity has been disputed since the 1980s.

caveats.text: Called the first Thai kingdom by convention, but Tai polities existed before it and the claim originates in later national historiography.

entities.summary: Tai kingdom of the upper Chao Phraya, traditionally cast as the first Thai state.

entities.name: Thonburi Kingdom
entities.summary: Fifteen years under Taksin, between the Burmese sack of Ayutthaya and the founding of the Chakri dynasty.

entities.name: Lan Xang
entities.date_note: Divided into Vientiane, Luang Phrabang and Champasak. Accounts differ on whether the break-up dates from 1694 or 1707.

alternatives.label: 1694, dating the split from the succession crisis

entities.summary: Lao kingdom of the middle Mekong, which broke into three rival successor kingdoms.

entities.name: Ngô Dynasty
entities.date_note: Sources give 965 or 968 for the end, depending on whether the interregnum of the twelve warlords is counted as part of the dynasty.
entities.summary: Founded after Bạch Đằng ended Chinese rule; collapsed into a period of warlords.

entities.name: Đinh Dynasty
entities.summary: Declared the state Đại Cồ Việt and an imperial title to match.

entities.name: Early Lê Dynasty
entities.summary: Repelled a Song invasion, then gave way to the Lý.

entities.name: Lý Dynasty
entities.date_note: The traditional account of the 1054 renaming has itself been questioned. Sources give 1225 or 1226 for the handover to the Trần.
entities.summary: Two centuries of consolidation; renamed the state Đại Việt in 1054.

entities.name: Trần Dynasty
entities.summary: Repelled three Mongol invasions.

entities.name: Hồ Dynasty
entities.summary: Seven years of forced reform; renamed the state Đại Ngu and fell to the Ming.

entities.name: Ming Occupation
entities.date_note: Ended by Lê Lợi's rising; the Lê dynasty dates from 1428.

name_forms.name: Jiaozhi
name_forms.note: The Ming province name. The period is also called the fourth Chinese domination.

entities.summary: Administered by the Ming as the province of Jiaozhi, not as a Vietnamese state at all.

entities.name: Later Lê Dynasty
entities.date_note: The Lê emperors became figureheads after 1533. The Trịnh in the north and the Nguyễn in the south are now authored beneath, as rivals to each other rather than as successive periods: they were simultaneous, and neither displaced the other — the Tây Sơn displaced both.
entities.summary: Nominally ruled for three and a half centuries, though for most of them real power lay with the Trịnh and Nguyễn lords.

links.note: Continued to claim the throne through the Mạc usurpation.

entities.name: Mạc Dynasty
entities.date_note: Driven from the capital in 1592; a rump state survived in the far north until 1677. Deliberately overlaps the Later Lê, because both claimed legitimacy at once.
entities.summary: Usurped the throne and held the north, overlapping the Lê rather than succeeding them.

links.note: Usurped the throne and held the north; the Lê claim continued against it.

entities.name: Tây Sơn Dynasty
entities.summary: A rising from the south that swept away the Trịnh, the Nguyễn lords and the Lê, and repelled a Qing invasion.

entities.name: Nguyễn Dynasty
entities.summary: The last dynasty; adopted the name Việt Nam, then ruled under French protection from the 1880s.

entities.name: French Indochina
entities.date_note: Formed in 1887 and dissolved in 1954 after Dien Bien Phu and the Geneva agreements.
entities.summary: The colonial union of Vietnamese, Cambodian and Lao territories.

entities.name: Medang Kingdom
entities.date_note: Also called Mataram, and not to be confused with the Islamic Mataram Sultanate of 1587-1755. Whether the Sailendra and Sanjaya lines were two dynasties, one, or a power-sharing arrangement is unresolved. The end is given as 1006 or 1016.

caveats.text: Frequently called Mataram, which collides with the later Islamic sultanate of the same name.

name_forms.name: Mataram Kingdom
name_forms.note: Ambiguous: the Islamic Mataram Sultanate is a different state six centuries later.

entities.summary: The Central Javanese period, which built Borobudur and Prambanan.

entities.name: Kahuripan
entities.date_note: The division produced Kediri and Janggala.
entities.summary: Airlangga's kingdom, divided between his sons at his abdication.

entities.name: Kediri Kingdom
entities.summary: East Javanese kingdom, remembered above all for its literature.

entities.name: Singhasari Kingdom
entities.summary: Displaced Kediri and expanded Javanese power outward; ended in the succession crisis that produced Majapahit.

entities.name: Demak Sultanate
entities.date_note: The end is given as either 1548 or 1554.
entities.summary: The first Islamic state on Java, and the power that finished Majapahit.

entities.name: Mataram Sultanate
entities.date_note: Ended with the Treaty of Giyanti in 1755, which split it between Yogyakarta and Surakarta. A different state from the Medang/Mataram kingdom of 732-1006.
entities.summary: The dominant Javanese state of the 17th century, partitioned under Dutch pressure.

entities.name: Aceh Sultanate
entities.date_note: Four founding dates circulate -- 1496, 1480, 1507 and 1514. Ended by Dutch conquest in 1903 after the Aceh War.
entities.summary: North Sumatran sultanate and a major pepper power, which fought the Dutch for three decades.

entities.name: Bruneian Empire
entities.date_note: Ends here in 1888, when Brunei became a British protectorate. The sultanate itself continues and is independent again from 1984, so this span covers its sovereign period rather than its existence -- running it unbroken to the present would assert a sovereignty that lapsed for ninety-six years.
entities.summary: Bornean sultanate that dominated the northwest coast before contracting under British and Sarawak pressure.

entities.name: Sultanate of Sulu
entities.date_note: Founding given as 1405 or 1457. Sovereignty was relinquished in 1915 under American administration.
entities.summary: Sultanate of the Sulu archipelago, which resisted Spanish control for three centuries.

entities.name: Tondo
entities.date_note: The 900 date comes from the Laguna Copperplate Inscription, which gives a floor rather than a founding. Other pre-colonial polities -- Cebu, Butuan, Maynila -- are much more thinly evidenced and are not authored here; the literature also contains the Code of Kalantiaw, a 1913 fabrication long treated as genuine, so claims in this area need checking one at a time.
entities.summary: Polity on Manila Bay, attested from 900 CE by the earliest surviving Philippine document.

entities.name: Second Turkic Khaganate
entities.date_note: Ended when the Uyghurs and their allies overthrew the last khagan.
entities.summary: Re-established Turkic power on the steppe after fifty years of Tang control, and left the Orkhon inscriptions.

entities.name: Saka
entities.date_note: Saka is what the Persians called them and Scythian is what the Greeks called a partly overlapping set of peoples. The two terms are not interchangeable and neither is a self-designation; what these groups called themselves is not settled. Entered as a people rather than a state, because no unified Saka polity is attested.

caveats.text: A Persian exonym overlapping the Greek exonym Scythian. Neither is what the people called themselves.

name_forms.name: Saka
name_forms.note: The Old Persian term.

entities.summary: Eastern Iranian steppe peoples, known by the Persian name for them.

entities.name: Sogdia
entities.date_note: No unified Sogdian kingdom is attested at any point: the cities acted independently under a succession of outside overlords, Achaemenid to Arab. The span marks the period of Sogdian cultural and commercial prominence, not the reign of a state.

caveats.text: A region and a culture rather than a polity. There was no Sogdian kingdom to have borders or a reign-list.

entities.summary: City-states around Samarkand and Bukhara whose merchants ran the Silk Road network. Never politically unified.

entities.name: Hephthalites
entities.date_note: Their origin, and whether the name covers a single people or a confederation, are both disputed. Broken around 560 by a Turkic and Sasanian alliance.

caveats.text: Whether the Hephthalites were one people or a confederation under one name is unresolved.

name_forms.name: White Huns
name_forms.note: A Greek and Latin usage. Their relation to the Huns of Europe is itself disputed.

entities.summary: Steppe power that dominated Bactria and pressed both Sasanian Iran and the Gupta empire.

entities.name: Uyghur Khaganate
entities.date_note: Ended when the Yenisei Kyrgyz sacked Ordu-Baliq in 840, scattering the Uyghurs south and west.
entities.summary: Steppe empire centred on Ordu-Baliq, and for a century the Tang dynasty's indispensable ally.

entities.name: Ghaznavid Empire
entities.date_note: Lost Khorasan to the Seljuks at Dandanaqan in 1040 and was thereafter an Afghan and north Indian power rather than an Iranian one. Held Khorasan, and briefly Ray and Hamadan, until Dandanaqan in 1040. After that it was an Afghan and north Indian power rather than an Iranian one.
entities.summary: Turkic dynasty ruling from Ghazna, whose raids into northern India opened the way for later Muslim rule there.

entities.name: Kara-Khanid Khanate
entities.date_note: The founding date is uncertain and usually given as around 840. Split into eastern and western branches, both eventually absorbed by the Qara Khitai and then the Khwarazmians.
entities.summary: The first Turkic dynasty to adopt Islam, ruling Transoxiana and Kashgaria.

entities.name: Khwarazmian Empire
entities.date_note: Ends with the death of Jalal al-Din in 1231, some years after the Mongols had broken the state itself.
entities.summary: Briefly the dominant power from Transoxiana to western Iran, destroyed by the Mongol invasion.

entities.name: Qara Khitai
entities.date_note: Chinese, Persian and Arab sources treat the Naiman usurpation of 1211 as the end of the dynasty; modern scholarship generally dates the state's fall to the Mongol conquest of 1218. Both are recorded.

alternatives.label: 1211, the Naiman usurpation
alternatives.note: The dynastic end in the traditional sources.

name_forms.name: Western Liao
name_forms.note: Names its descent from the Liao dynasty of northern China.

entities.summary: Khitan successor state in Central Asia, founded by refugees from the fall of the Liao.

entities.name: Khanate of Bukhara
entities.summary: Uzbek state in Transoxiana; an emirate from 1785 and a Russian protectorate from 1868.

entities.name: Khanate of Khiva
entities.summary: Uzbek khanate on the lower Amu Darya, a Russian protectorate from 1873.

entities.name: Khanate of Kokand
entities.date_note: Dated from 1709 or from 1798, depending on whether the earlier principality is counted as the khanate.
entities.summary: Ferghana valley khanate, annexed outright by Russia rather than left as a protectorate.

entities.name: Russian Conquest of Central Asia
entities.date_note: Tashkent fell in 1865, Bukhara became a protectorate in 1868, Khiva in 1873, and Kokand was annexed in 1876; the border settlements ran to the 1890s.
entities.summary: Russian annexation of the three khanates, closing the last independent steppe polities.

entities.name: Arab Conquest of Iran
entities.date_note: Nahavand in 642 was the decisive engagement; the conventional end is the death of the last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, in 651.
entities.summary: Eighteen years that ended the Sasanian empire and began the Islamic period in Iran.

entities.name: The Iranian Intermezzo
entities.date_note: Not a coinage of this dataset: Britannica uses 'the Iranian intermezzo' as a section heading for this period. It is a framing rather than a polity, and the dynasties inside it overlapped and fought each other.
entities.summary: Native Iranian dynasties ruling between Arab and Turkic domination.

entities.name: Tahirid Dynasty
entities.summary: Governed Khorasan from Nishapur, nominally for the Abbasids and in practice for themselves.

entities.name: Saffarid Dynasty
entities.date_note: The end is given as 1002 or 1003, with the Ghaznavid conquest.
entities.summary: Rose from Sistan under a coppersmith turned warlord and briefly threatened Baghdad itself.

entities.name: Buyid Dynasty
entities.date_note: Entered Baghdad in 945. The arrangement left the caliphate intact as an institution while removing its power, which is why the Abbasid line continues past this point in the dataset.
entities.summary: Shia dynasty from the Caspian highlands that took Baghdad and ruled through the Abbasid caliphs it kept as figureheads.

entities.name: Qara Qoyunlu
entities.summary: Turkoman confederation holding Azerbaijan and western Iran.

entities.name: Aq Qoyunlu
entities.date_note: Ended when Ismail I took Tabriz in 1501, which is also the Safavid founding: one event, two entries.
entities.summary: Turkoman confederation that displaced the Qara Qoyunlu and was in turn displaced by the Safavids.

entities.name: Afsharid Dynasty
entities.date_note: Founded in 1736 when Nader deposed the last Safavid. After his assassination in 1747 the dynasty held only Khorasan, under his grandson Shahrokh, until the Qajar victory in 1796.
entities.summary: Nader Shah's conquest state, which outlasted him only in Khorasan.

links.note: Held Khorasan after 1747 while the Zand held the rest of Iran.

entities.name: Zand Dynasty
entities.date_note: Encyclopaedia Iranica gives 1751-94; Britannica gives 1750-79, which counts only Karim Khan's own rule. He never took the title shahanshah, governing as vakil for a Safavid figurehead. Overlaps the Afsharids, who held Khorasan throughout.
entities.summary: Ruled Iran except Khorasan from Shiraz, remembered for an unusually peaceful reign.

links.note: Held Iran except Khorasan, which remained Afsharid.

entities.name: Late Bronze Age Canaanite Phase
entities.summary: The cities under Egyptian and Hittite overlordship, before the collapse that freed them.

entities.name: Phoenician Independence
entities.date_note: Begins with the collapse rather than with any Phoenician event. Ends as Assyrian pressure resumes under Ashurnasirpal II.
entities.summary: Three centuries of genuine autonomy after the Bronze Age Collapse removed the empires above them — the period of the alphabet and the western voyages.

entities.name: Under Assyria
entities.summary: Tributary to Assyria, with the cities retaining their kings.

entities.name: Under Babylon
entities.summary: Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Tyre for thirteen years.

entities.name: Under Persia
entities.summary: Achaemenid subjects supplying the imperial navy, still ruled by their own kings — which is why 539 is the wrong place to end Phoenicia.

entities.name: Byblos
entities.date_note: Occupied far earlier than the Phoenician period proper; the start marks its Egyptian trade rather than a founding.
entities.summary: The oldest of the cities and the earliest to dominate, trading cedar with Egypt from the third millennium.

entities.name: Sidon
entities.summary: Held primacy between the Byblian and Tyrian phases, and revolted against Persia in the 350s.

entities.name: Tyre
entities.summary: Dominant from the tenth century, founded Carthage and the western colonies, and fell to Alexander after a seven-month siege.

entities.name: Arwad
entities.summary: The northernmost city, on an island off the Syrian coast.

entities.name: Early Vedic (Rigvedic)
entities.date_note: Dated linguistically. Witzel subdivides the Rigvedic period into three stages on the internal stratigraphy of the language. No excavated horizon dates these texts.
entities.summary: The period of the Rigveda: pastoral, mobile, and in the northwest.

entities.name: Later Vedic
entities.date_note: The Painted Grey Ware horizon is associated with this phase in particular, roughly 1200-600 BCE — not with the Vedic period as a whole, which is what a single undivided block implied.
entities.summary: Eastward settlement into the Ganges plain, iron, larger polities, and the Brahmanas and early Upanishads.

entities.name: The Vedic Corpus
entities.date_note: Relative order is firm; absolute dates are not. The Rigveda is the best anchored, partly through the Mitanni synchronism; the Upanishads are the least, with proposals spanning 700 BCE to 100 CE.
entities.summary: Rigveda, then the other three Vedas, the Brahmanas, and the Upanishads.

entities.name: Trịnh Lords (Đàng Ngoài)
entities.date_note: The Lê dynasty continued as the source of legitimacy throughout, which is why this sits under it rather than beside it. Ended by the Tây Sơn.
entities.summary: Ruled the north in the Lê emperor's name, holding real power for two and a half centuries.

links.note: Fought the Nguyễn for the country while both claimed to serve the same emperor.

entities.name: Nguyễn Lords (Đàng Trong)
entities.date_note: Nominally subordinate to the same Lê emperor as the Trịnh, and at war with them for much of the period. Ended by the Tây Sơn, from whom the surviving Nguyễn later took the throne outright in 1802.
entities.summary: Ruled the south independently in practice, expanding into the Mekong delta at Cham and Khmer expense.

links.note: Fought the Trịnh for the country while both claimed to serve the same emperor.

entities.name: Liao Dynasty
entities.date_note: Two founding dates are both defensible and both in use. 907 is traditional and the year Yelü Abaoji became khagan; 916 is when he proclaimed himself emperor in the Chinese manner, which most Chinese scholarship prefers. A Shandong University study argues the Liaoshi's own use of 907 was deliberate rather than an error. Ended 1125 when Jurchen forces captured Emperor Tianzuo.

alternatives.label: 916, the imperial proclamation
alternatives.note: When Abaoji took the title huangdi, proclaimed an era name and built a Confucian temple.

alternatives.label: 907, the traditional date
alternatives.note: The Liaoshi's own date, which Britannica leads with.

name_forms.name: Khitan Empire
name_forms.note: The founding state was the Great Khitan State, 大契丹; the Chinese-style dynastic name came later.

entities.summary: Khitan empire ruling Manchuria, Mongolia and the northern edge of the North China Plain, governed through separate steppe and Chinese administrations.

entities.name: Jin Dynasty (Jurchen)
entities.date_note: Founded 1115 by Wanyan Aguda; ended with the fall of Caizhou in February 1234 under Mongol attack. Distinct from the earlier Jin (晉, 266-420) despite the identical English spelling.

name_forms.name: Chin
name_forms.note: Wade-Giles renders this dynasty and the earlier Jin (晉) identically, so the older romanisation cannot tell them apart.

name_forms.name: Jurchen Jin
name_forms.note: Used in English to separate it from the Jin of 266-420.

entities.summary: Jurchen empire that took northern China from the Song, ruling from Kaifeng until the Mongol conquest.

entities.name: Jingkang Incident
entities.date_note: Britannica dates the incident across 1126-1127. The surviving prince fled south and took the throne as Gaozong, which is why this dataset's Song splits at 1127.
entities.summary: Jin forces sacked Kaifeng and carried off emperors Huizong and Qinzong, ending the Northern Song.

entities.name: Western Xia
entities.date_note: Founded 1038 when Li Yuanhao declared himself emperor, though Tangut autonomy in the region long predates that. Destroyed by the Mongols in 1227, the year Genghis Khan died. Unlike Liao, Jin and Song, it received no official history from the Yuan, which is a fact about the historiography rather than about the state.

name_forms.name: Xi Xia
name_forms.note: The form Britannica files it under.

entities.summary: Tangut state in the northwest, with its own script and no official dynastic history.

entities.name: Xia Dynasty
entities.date_note: The 2070-1600 BCE span comes from the state-sponsored Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project, which identifies the Xia with the Erlitou culture. Those dates should be read as that project's position rather than as an established chronology; Britannica treats the dynasty as legendary and the Cambridge History of Ancient China begins with the Shang.

caveats.text: Britannica describes the Xia as legendary, and the Cambridge History of Ancient China starts its account at the Shang.
The Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project assigns the Xia 2070-1600 BCE and identifies every Erlitou phase with it. Its method drew sustained criticism in Western sinology.

entities.summary: Traditionally the first Chinese dynasty. Whether it existed as a state is disputed.

entities.name: Multi-Regional Empires
entities.date_note: The span runs from the Achaemenids to the Hong Kong handover and is a container rather than a claim. Each empire here is also reachable from every region it held, so a reader browsing Anatolia or the Nile finds the Ottomans without coming here first. Grouping the caliphates, the Mongols and the European maritime empires for comparison is a deliberate scholarly move: Burbank and Cooper treat them as comparable, and the Oxford World History of Empire frames the comparison as a corrective to older single-region imperial history.
entities.summary: Polities that held territory in more than one world region, gathered so they can be compared with each other.

caveats.text: Called multi-regional, not cross-regional: these polities were in several regions at once rather than crossing from one to another.

entities.name: Namazga Sequence
entities.date_note: RECEIVED FRAMEWORK, NOT A DATED ONE. The phases in general circulation are Namazga I 4800-4000, II 4000-3500, III 3500-3000, IV 3000-2500, V 2500-2200 and VI 2200-1500 BCE, and competing bracket sets exist for most of them. They descend from Masson's Soviet-era ceramic typology; no published radiocarbon table for Namazga-depe itself supports them. Where independent dating does exist it disagrees: modern reassessments compress the Namazga V urban phase into roughly 2400-1950 or 2250-1700 BCE, and one report gives C14 dates for a single final Namazga VI layer scattering from 1884 to 818 BC. Use the phase names to talk to the literature; do not use these numbers as dates.

caveats.text: These phase brackets are a typological convention, not measurements. Treating Namazga V as a dated period rather than a pottery style is the standard error.

entities.summary: The six-phase framework that every account of Central Asian prehistory is written in, and which rests on pottery typology rather than radiocarbon.

entities.name: Kelteminar Culture
entities.date_note: A peer-reviewed source places Kelteminar in the sixth to fourth millennia BC in general terms, and that is the whole of the defensible dating. No site-level radiocarbon dataset with lab numbers was locatable for any Kelteminar site, and the field disagrees about the culture's geographic and temporal boundaries — the authors of that paper decline to label their own 9200-7800 cal BP material at Toda-1 Cave as Kelteminar for that reason.
entities.summary: Hunter-fisher-gatherers of the Aral basin and the Amu Darya delta, in contact with the farming villages to their south.

entities.name: Altyn-Depe
entities.date_note: Dated by its Namazga V pottery, so it inherits that sequence's problem entirely. The excavator's own figures — Early Namazga V c. 2100-1850 BC, Late c. 1850-1650 — are typological. No modern radiocarbon programme for the site was locatable, so nothing here is independent of the ceramic framework.
entities.summary: A walled town of the Namazga culture with a stepped tower, craft quarters and trade reaching Mundigak and Shahr-i Sokhta.

entities.name: Epipalaeolithic (Levant)
entities.date_note: Calibrated to IntCal20. Its end at 10,000 BC is exactly where 'Mesolithic (Eurasia)' starts, and that is the point: the two are largely the same idea under different regional naming traditions, not adjacent periods. This entry exists because the EARLY part, back to 23,000 BC, sits inside the Palaeolithic band where nothing else names it. Absolute figures vary by several centuries across calibration vintages.

caveats.text: Not a separate stage from the Mesolithic: the Near East, North Africa and southern Europe say Epipalaeolithic where northern Europe says Mesolithic.

entities.summary: The long Levantine hunter-gatherer sequence between the Upper Palaeolithic and farming, ending where the Mesolithic begins.

entities.name: Kebaran
entities.date_note: The Oxford IntCal20 table gives 23,000-16,000 cal BC for the Early Epipalaeolithic as a whole. Kebaran-only figures differ across sources (c. 18,000-14,500 BP on the coast), and no single end date is settled.
entities.summary: The Early Epipalaeolithic of the Levant: small mobile groups with microlithic toolkits, through the Last Glacial Maximum.

entities.name: Geometric Kebaran
entities.summary: The Middle Epipalaeolithic, named for its geometric microliths, between the Kebaran and the Natufian.

entities.name: Chalcolithic (Southeast Europe)
entities.date_note: Copper minerals are worked from c. 6200 BC and native copper from c. 5500 BC, but the Chalcolithic proper begins with smelting at c. 5000 BC. Belovode in Serbia holds the earliest securely dated smelting anywhere, and specialists expect that status to move. There is no global Chalcolithic node, deliberately. Most of sub-Saharan Africa goes from stone straight to iron; China folds early copper into the Late Neolithic; the Americas never reached a continent-wide Bronze Age; and Australian archaeology has dropped three-age terminology altogether.

caveats.text: A Copper Age is not a universal stage. Most of sub-Saharan Africa has none at all, moving from stone tools directly to iron.

entities.summary: The Balkan Copper Age: the world's earliest known copper smelting, and the gold of the Varna cemetery.

entities.name: Chalcolithic (Southern Levant)
entities.date_note: c. 4700/4500-3700/3600 cal BC is the most consistently defended range; some syntheses broaden it to 5000-3500 BC. Both internal boundaries are described in the literature as imprecisely dated, and whether the Chalcolithic overlaps Early Bronze I is disputed. There is no global Chalcolithic node, deliberately. Most of sub-Saharan Africa goes from stone straight to iron; China folds early copper into the Late Neolithic; the Americas never reached a continent-wide Bronze Age; and Australian archaeology has dropped three-age terminology altogether.
entities.summary: The southern Levantine Copper Age, with copper hoards, ossuary burial and the Ghassulian culture.

entities.name: Chalcolithic (Anatolia)
entities.date_note: c. 5500-3000 BC is the most commonly defended whole-period range, but at least three incompatible sub-periodizations are in active use for Central, Eastern and Western Anatolia, differing by centuries. Treat any single Anatolian figure with caution. There is no global Chalcolithic node, deliberately. Most of sub-Saharan Africa goes from stone straight to iron; China folds early copper into the Late Neolithic; the Americas never reached a continent-wide Bronze Age; and Australian archaeology has dropped three-age terminology altogether.
entities.summary: The Anatolian Copper Age, spanning the long interval between the Neolithic villages and the Early Bronze Age.

entities.name: Late Chalcolithic (Mesopotamia)
entities.date_note: In Mesopotamian usage 'Chalcolithic' covers the pre-Bronze sequence, and the narrower Late Chalcolithic runs c. 4500-3100 BC. Note this ends 200 years AFTER the global Bronze Age node begins at 3300 BC: the regional Bronze Age does not start until Uruk closes. There is no global Chalcolithic node, deliberately. Most of sub-Saharan Africa goes from stone straight to iron; China folds early copper into the Late Neolithic; the Americas never reached a continent-wide Bronze Age; and Australian archaeology has dropped three-age terminology altogether.
entities.summary: Terminal Ubaid through Late Uruk, the LC1-LC5 sequence that ends with the first cities and the first writing.

entities.name: Chalcolithic (South Asia)
entities.date_note: No single pan-Indian range is defensible. These cultures run c. 3000/2600 BC to c. 700 BC and are CONTEMPORARY with, not prior to, mature Harappan Bronze Age urbanism elsewhere in the subcontinent — which is why no global Chalcolithic node can exist. Jorwe alone runs to c. 700 BC, inside the global Iron Age band. There is no global Chalcolithic node, deliberately. Most of sub-Saharan Africa goes from stone straight to iron; China folds early copper into the Late Neolithic; the Americas never reached a continent-wide Bronze Age; and Australian archaeology has dropped three-age terminology altogether.

caveats.text: Not the stage between Neolithic and Bronze Age here: South Asian Chalcolithic cultures coexist with Bronze Age cities nearby.

entities.summary: The Deccan and central Indian copper-using farming cultures — Kayatha, Ahar-Banas, Malwa and Jorwe — which are not a pre-Bronze stage at all.

entities.name: East Asian Prehistory
entities.summary: Jomon Japan and the Chinese Neolithic, gathered here for browsing. Both also sit in their own national sequences, where they belong.
entities.date_note: A navigation era. It makes no dating claim of its own: the span is the extent of the entries gathered under it, each of which carries its own dating and sources. Jomon's primary home stays under Japan, because it is Japan's founding era rather than a detachable prehistoric episode.

entities.name: Oceanian Prehistory
entities.summary: The Pleistocene settlement of Sahul and the Lapita expansion into the Pacific, gathered here for browsing.
entities.date_note: A navigation era making no dating claim of its own. Aboriginal Australia is deliberately NOT gathered here: it has no end date because the traditions are living, and filing an ongoing culture under 'prehistory' would say something false. Its dated Pleistocene sites appear instead.
